why: Application support is judged on how incidents are handled: speed, communication and preventing repeats. ITIL vocabulary and ServiceNow appear in most support job offers.
outcome: classify and prioritise incidents, run an incident calmly with clear updates, write a post-mortem, and use ITIL terms correctly.

lessons.title: ITIL essentials
text: ITIL is a framework of good practices for IT services. In support roles you will mostly use four practices: incident, problem, change and service request management.
The key difference: an incident is about restoring service fast; a problem is about finding and removing the underlying cause.
points: Incident: unplanned interruption or degradation of a service.
Service request: a normal request (access, password reset), not a failure.
Problem: the cause of one or more incidents; a known error has a documented workaround.
Change: any modification to production, assessed for risk (standard, normal, emergency).
SLA: agreed targets with the client, e.g. P1 response in 15 min, resolution in 4 h.

lessons.title: Handle an incident
text: Priority = impact (how many users or how critical the service) × urgency (how fast it hurts). Agree the matrix in advance so nobody debates it at 3 a.m.
During a major incident, separate roles: someone fixes, someone coordinates and communicates. Regular updates calm everyone, even when there is no news yet.
points: Log the ticket first, with time, symptoms, impact and who reported it.
Check what changed recently: deployments, config, certificates, data volumes.
Restore first (rollback, restart, failover, workaround), investigate deeply later.
Update stakeholders on a fixed rhythm (every 30 min for a P1) with: impact, what we know, next step, next update time.
Escalate early with facts, not late with excuses.

example.code:
[P1 UPDATE 10:30] Job search unavailable for all users since 09:52.
Cause under investigation; a deployment at 09:45 is the main suspect.
Action: rollback in progress, ETA 10:45.
Next update: 11:00 or earlier if resolved.

lessons.title: Root cause and post-mortem
text: Once service is back, open a problem to find the root cause so it does not happen again. Techniques: 5 Whys, timeline reconstruction, fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram.
A blameless post-mortem focuses on how the system allowed the failure, not on who made a mistake. It ends with concrete actions, owners and dates.
points: Timeline: detection, response, mitigation, resolution, with timestamps.
Measure MTTD (time to detect) and MTTR (time to restore).
Actions: fix the cause, improve detection (alerts), improve response (runbooks).
Write the known error and workaround in the knowledge base.

example.code:
5 Whys
1. Why was search down? The API returned 500 errors.
2. Why? It could not connect to the database.
3. Why? The connection pool was exhausted.
4. Why? A new feature opened connections without closing them.
5. Why? No load test or code review check covered connection handling.
Actions: fix the leak, add a pool-usage alert, add a load test to CI.

items: Service broken or degraded → restore fast
Critical service down for many users
Who / what is affected since when

pitfalls: Investigating root cause for an hour while users are still blocked: restore first.
Silence during an incident; stakeholders assume the worst.
Closing the incident without opening a problem for recurring issues.
Blame in post-mortems, which makes people hide information next time.

exercises.q: Payroll export fails for one office the day before payday; others work. What priority and why?
exercises.answer: High (P2, possibly P1 depending on the matrix): impact is limited to one office, but urgency is very high because salaries are due tomorrow. Priority combines both.

exercises.q: Write a first status message for a login outage affecting all users since 14:05.
exercises.answer: [P1] Since 14:05, users cannot log in to the application. The team is investigating; recent changes are being checked. Workaround: none yet. Next update at 14:45.

exercises.q: The same disk-full incident happened 4 times this month. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Open a problem record, find the root cause (log rotation missing, growing table, temp files), apply a permanent fix, add an alert at 80% disk usage, and document the known error and workaround meanwhile.

interview.a: An incident is an unplanned interruption that we restore as quickly as possible. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents, which we investigate to prevent them from happening again.

interview.q: Tell me how you handled a critical incident.
interview.a: Use STAR: the situation and impact, your role, the actions (log, assess, communicate, restore, escalate), and the result with numbers (restored in 40 minutes), then what you improved afterwards.
With an impact × urgency matrix agreed with the business and aligned with SLAs, then by SLA deadline. I re-evaluate when new information changes the impact.
